
=================================================================
#56 Exile  (655)
Arc: The Fall of Euija · place: mugun · tone: exile drama — into island folklore
Logline: Three years of mourning, by the rite. Everyone in Sabi knows exactly what can be done inside them.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ **Queen Satek** dies, and the king, her son, loses the right to say no.
[1] [MAP 655: ]
[2] ¶ Three years of mourning, by the rite. The king may not judge, may not sign, may not overturn. Everyone in Sabi knows exactly how long three years is, and exactly what can be done inside them.
[3] ❝QUOTE (Stele of Satek Jijeok (砂宅智積碑), Buyeo, 654 — Buyeo National Museum) [Minister Satek]: Ninth day of the first month, year of the Wood Tiger. Satek Jijuk of Naji Fortress, grieving that the body’s days go so easily and its months come back so hard, cut gold to build a precious hall and carved jade to raise a treasure pagoda.❞
[4] ¶ Minister Satek carved that last year, grieving his own short days. He knows what mourning is good for.
[5] ¶ The Queen was Satek. Her death removes the clan’s hand from the king’s sleeve, and the clan understands, before the funeral rites are finished, that the sleeve is now free.
[6] ¶ With her gone, the clan has one worry left. The king owns a man who cannot be bought: Hundred-Victories **Gyebek**. And Gyebek owns a horse.
[7] ¶ They have watched him work. On the border, Gyebek earned his nickname mostly one way. He leaves the line to other men and goes looking for the general. His black horse, Gomanari, is the fastest thing on four legs in Samhan. Gyebek rides him flat along the neck like a thrown knife, the blade reversed along his forearm. The general sees a black shape where the field was empty. He starts to turn his horse, and does not finish turning. One cut on the pass. By the time the escort draws, the black horse is a speck on the far ridge. An army stands in a field with nobody left to tell it what to do.
[8] Elder Satek: He doesn’t ride at armies. / He rides at one man. / When the mourning’s over, whose house do you suppose that horse turns toward.
[9] ¶ Gyebek has no clan. That is the whole problem. He has a wife the king found for him, and a boy and a girl who carry the name the king made up. He took the wife and the name the way he takes orders, and has kept both. A man with a clan can be bargained with: you find out what his family wants and give them some of it. A man with no clan wants only what the king wants, and there is nothing to buy.
[10] ── SCENE: The Monastery ──
[11] ¶ So the two largest houses in Baekje meet, which has not happened in living memory except across a body.
[12] ¶ They meet at night, at a monastery that belongs to neither of them, and each brings the same number of men, counted twice at the gate by both sides.
[13] Elder Satek: Lord Yunbi. How many generations have we been at this?
[14] Elder Yunbi: Four. / Two of the three who died at the lantern festival last year were my nephews.
[15] Elder Satek: One of them was my grandson.
[16] ¶ Neither of them apologises. Nobody expected it and it would have ended the meeting.
[17] ¶ Halfway through the wine, a servant finds a second set of footprints behind the monastery screen — too small for the counted guards, too careful for a pilgrim. Yunbi’s man and Satek’s man look at each other and, for once, do not accuse. Someone is listening for a third house. Or for the king.
[18] Elder Satek: Spill the cups. / Tonight the doors matter more than the words.
[19] Elder Yunbi: So why did you send for me tonight.
[20] Elder Satek: His Majesty has more than forty sons. / Where do you imagine he means to seat them.
[21] Elder Yunbi: …In our chairs.
[22] Elder Satek: In the chairs of all eight houses.
[23] ¶ It goes quiet. Outside, the two sets of men are standing apart in the courtyard, arranged by habit into the shape of a fight.
[24] Elder Yunbi: We will destroy each other and lose everything. / …For how long.
[25] Elder Satek: As long as it takes. / After that we go back to the way we were.
[26] Elder Yunbi: Agreed. / What gets removed first.
[27] Elder Satek: The one with no house.
[28] ¶ They do not say his name at the table. Two houses that have not agreed on anything since before the capital moved agree, in under an hour, on one soldier with no family — and the agreement is written down nowhere, because agreements like that never are.
[29] Elder Satek: There is no price on that man.
[30] Elder Satek: Things without a price get removed.
[31] ── SCENE: The Offer ──
[32] ¶ They try the ordinary way first: they offer him a name. A real one, an old one, the eighth branch of a minor house, papers and a grave-line and ancestors, and a clan chair at the end of it for his son. It is a serious offer, and it is the only thing he has ever wanted.
[33] Elder Satek: Think of the boy. / He grows up with a name the king invented. Every door in Sabi will know it.
[34] Gyebek: I have thought of him. / …I already have one.
[35] Elder Satek: The king made that one up.
[36] Gyebek: Yes. Which is why it is owed to someone.
[37] ── SCENE: The Drill Ground ──
[38] ¶ The arrow comes through a tent wall at the Ungjin drill ground and takes the man standing next to him, who was taller. Nobody is ever charged. The fletching is Baekje army issue, which narrows it to about nine thousand people, which is the point of using it.
[39] ¶ He stops eating food he has not watched being cooked. He sleeps in a different room each night, which the ministers immediately report to the regency as the behaviour of a man planning something.
[40] ¶ One minister comes to see him: Sungchung, the man at court who asks the questions nobody else will.
[41] Sungchung: General. You should be away from here. / Half a year. Until His Majesty is out of mourning.
[42] Gyebek: …I don’t run.
[43] Sungchung: Which is exactly how they win.
[44] ¶ The truce holds exactly as long as it needs to. Four generations of blood, suspended for the length of one signature, and both houses will go back to burning each other’s carts before the year is out.
[45] ── SCENE: The Sealed Order ──
[46] ¶ Gyebek is summoned to the hall and told to kneel, and the order is read out over his head.
[47] ¶ The order is genuine. That is the craftsmanship of it. It bears the royal seal, because a king in mourning leaves his seal with the Assembly so that the country does not stop, and the Assembly has had it for four months.
[48] ¶ It is read with the king’s formula and the king’s seal, but not in the king’s voice. **Minister Satek** holds the Assembly’s borrowed stamp.
[49] Minister Satek: The seal is set. / I read this in the Assembly’s name. / Gyebek is hereby sent into exile!
[50] Satek Chunbok: …It is His Majesty’s will.
[51] ¶ Remember the young Satek who just called it His Majesty’s will. He has small feet, and he walks very carefully. He will say worse things in His Majesty’s name, later, to a much bigger king.
[52] Gyebek: His Majesty is in mourning. / He cannot will anything.
[53] ¶ Nobody answers him. He is correct, and it is not the kind of correct that helps.
[54] ¶ He is put on the boat the same afternoon. Satek water at the berth; a Yunbi winter contract in the captain’s sleeve. Even exile borrows a clan harbour.
[55] ¶ His wife is at the berth with a bundle and both children. Nobody sent for her. In Sabi, news of a sealed order travels faster than the order.
[56] Gyebek’s Wife: How long.
[57] Gyebek: I do not know.
[58] Gyebek’s Wife: Guess. For the children. / Say any number.
[59] Gyebek: I do not know the number. / I will not give them a wrong one.
[60] Gyebek’s Wife: …No. You wouldn’t.
[61] ¶ The boy asks if Father is going to war. Gyebek says no, because it is not a war. It is the only question all day he can answer exactly.
[62] ── SCENE: Sabi ──
[63] ¶ In Sabi, the order comes back to the king that evening, to be filed. That is the insult. His own seal sits at the bottom, a little crooked.
[64] King Euija: Who. / Who used my seal — / Who took my man —
[65] Minister Satek: Your Majesty… the Assembly— / In mourning the council—
[66] King Euija: Minister Satek! / I swear I’ll just— overturn the whole lot of them like Gesomun did!! / You put my man on a boat? You used my mourning as a gap?
[67] King Euija: Minister. How many days are left of my rite?
[68] Minister Satek: …Nine hundred and seventy-two, Majesty.
[69] King Euija: Good. Count them. Out loud, at my door, every morning, so I never lose one. / The morning it reaches nothing, I call the Assembly. All eight houses. Every chair. / Then I send a boat. Well? Start.
[70] Minister Satek: …Nine hundred and seventy-two.
[71] ¶ Euija laughs first, the way he always does. Then he makes the minister say it again.
[72] ── SCENE: Tamla ──
[73] ¶ He wakes on a beach with sand in his teeth and no idea how many days it has been. The not-knowing is worse than the beach.
[74] [PLACE mugun: The island where Baekje sends men it can’t afford to kill.]
[75] [CARD Yuri Dora: Yuri Dora, king of Tamla. He tells stories to men nobody else will talk to.]
[76] Gyebek: How many days.
[77] Yuri Dora: Ah. Not one for greetings, then.
[78] Gyebek: …How many days.
[79] Yuri Dora: Eleven. Better?
[80] ¶ It is better. Visibly. The islanders will spend five years noticing that this man is calmed by numbers and unsettled by almost everything else.
[81] ¶ He takes eleven from a number he has carried since the hall.
[82] Gyebek: Nine hundred and sixty-one.
[83] Yuri Dora: Until what?
[84] Gyebek: Until His Majesty can sign again. / Then he sends for me.
[85] Yuri Dora: Ha. A man who carries his own calendar. / Your name?
[86] Gyebek: I am called Gyebek.
[87] Yuri Dora: Gyebek? Like geobuk? A man named Turtle?
[88] Gyebek: No. _Gye_ is the stone step, and _baek_ is the eldest.
[89] Yuri Dora: …It was a joke.
[90] Gyebek: …Ah.
[91] ¶ He says _ah_ the way another man would say _I will write that down_. It would be a mistake to read the pause as slowness; somewhere behind those eyes, a ledger has just gained a line.
[92] ¶ **First night on the island. A fire, two cups, and a storyteller who never asks permission. “Sit or don’t. Once there were two suns…”**
